question.text: A ratchet / anti-dilution clause in an AIF investment agreement is triggered when:

answer.text: The investee company raises a follow-on round at a higher valuation than the AIF's entry price
The investee company raises a follow-on round at a lower valuation than the AIF's entry price (a 'down round'), causing dilution
The investee company declares its first dividend
The fund manager rotates the portfolio manager assigned to the deal

explanation.text: The Logic: A ratchet / anti-dilution clause is triggered by a future down round — a subsequent issuance of shares at a price lower than the AIF's entry price. The workbook describes the protection as additional shares being issued to the AIF to offset the dilution caused by the cheaper share issuance. The Trap: Anti-dilution does not engage when valuations move up, when dividends are paid, or when personnel changes occur at the manager. It is specifically a down-round protection mechanism on the investee company's cap table. Note: Rewritten as a generic down-round / ratchet protection item. The original options described weighted-average anti-dilution (price weighted by old- and new-round shares) and broad-based vs narrow-based variants, none of which the checked workbook defines.
